title: Brake pad change: push two pads flush into their retainers each side of the disc, then swing the caliper down over them
instruction: Fit the new brake pads, then swing the caliper down over them.
context: A brake pad change as a technician does it on a car on a stand: wheel removed, the front corner still under its fender, so the hands reach in through the wheel arch past the inner liner, strut and control arm. In the maker's order, with the caliper pivoted up on its upper guide pin, each new pad is pushed 12 mm into its two sprung retainers until flush; then the 2 kg caliper is swung down over them, its bridge closing over the pads' edges with 1 mm: a pad standing proud stops it short. Replacing brakes is a core task of automotive service technicians (O*NET 49-3023: 'Repair, reline, replace, and adjust brakes'); the pad change is the most common brake job. Modelled at the scale of a Honda Jazz front corner.
setup: Two YAM arms at the near edge of the table; positions are (x forward from the arm bases, y left) in cm, heights above the table. A front corner of a small hatchback (Honda Jazz class) with its wheel removed stands on the table as it would on a stand, seen from the car's side: the hub face and wheel studs toward the arms, a vented disc 262 mm across and 21 mm thick, its axis along x, centred at (44, -15) and 25 cm up. Around it, as static solid parts: the fender panel (a plate 4 mm thick standing at x 35, with the wheel arch cut out of it, arch radius 35.5 cm about the hub, the panel cut away on the car's end side beyond 110 degrees of the arch), the inner arch liner (a sheet arc of radius 38 cm about the hub, from the sill to 150 degrees, running 39 cm back), the MacPherson strut (damper 54 mm, coil spring 125 mm across) on its clamp on the knuckle, the lower control arm from the knuckle's ball joint back to two bushings, the tie rod, and the bulkhead behind. The bracket on the disc's arm-side rim carries four greased stainless pad retainers, two each side of the disc. The single-piston floating caliper (about 2 kg) hangs on its upper guide pin, pivoted up 150 degrees out of the way, its piston already pushed back; its lower guide bolt is out. Two new pads (131 x 55 x 15 mm with ears and steel backing plates, 0.2 kg each) stand on one ear, linings towards the disc's side they belong to, in a slotted wooden parts box (70 x 100 mm, 12 cm tall) on the table at (26, 2). The wheel arch is the only way in: the hands go in through it, under the raised caliper.
scoring: Photo, feeler gauge and inspection. 1.0, held for 2 s: both pads seated flush in their own retainers, the inner pad (shim and wear indicator) on the piston's side and the outer on the fingers' side, both linings facing the disc (pushed the full 12 mm in: a 1 mm feeler gauge does not enter between any ear and its retainer's end), the caliper swung down and shut over them (within 1 degree), and no gripper within 5 cm of the pads or the caliper's bridge. 0.3: both pads flush, without the 1.0 result. 0.1: one pad flush. The pads must be flush before the caliper comes down: a caliper that pushes a pad home does not count (0.3 at most). 0 otherwise. A pad dropped off the bench caps the score at 0.1.
reset_notes: The pads back in their slots in the parts box, the caliper pivoted back up to 150 degrees on its pin. No seed changes the scene.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz, GPU. Fender arch (R 35.5 cm), inner liner (R 38 cm, estimates), strut, control arm, tie rod and bulkhead are static solids sized from a Honda Jazz (GD). Simplified: fender cut away beyond 110 degrees of the arch on the car's end, no skirt, hub not turned to lock. Caliper hung up at 150 degrees, pin friction 1.3 N m. Clip channels 1.5 mm wider each side than real; no spring drag. Piston pre-pushed; hose, lower bolt and torque left out. Mass and drag estimated.
